query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A minor Hf addition (approximately 1–2 atomic percent) to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will promote the in situ formation of stable HfO2 oxide dispersions that enhance creep resistance and corrosion stability while maintaining the alloy’s balanced strength and ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA with a fine, uniform lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure that exhibits high fracture strength and moderate ductility, with demonstrated mechanical performance up to 700°C.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor Hf addition (approximately 1–2 at%) into the alloy composition during melting/casting.
generation.conditions: Performance evaluated under ambient conditions, under cyclic thermal fluctuations up to 700°C, and in corrosive environments representative of aerospace/spacecraft service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Nano-sized, in situ formed HfO2 oxide dispersions located at lamellar interfaces.
generation.mechanism: The alloying Hf has a strong affinity for oxygen, leading to the formation of stable HfO2 dispersoids during processing. These dispersoids can impede dislocation motion and grain boundary sliding, thus enhancing long-term creep resistance. Additionally, they act as barriers reducing corrosive pathways, thereby improving corrosion stability without compromising the ductile and strong lamellar structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved long-term creep resistance and corrosion protection compared to the as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, with only minimal changes in room-temperature strength and ductility.
generation.baseline: The as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy exhibits a fracture strength near 1.2 GPa, ~22–25% elongation at room temperature, and stable performance up to 700°C.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected only within a narrow Hf addition range (around 1–2 at%). Excessive Hf could lead to embrittlement or unwanted phase formation, while too little may not produce sufficient oxide dispersions for impact.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal Hf concentration and the quantitative improvement in creep and corrosion performance remain uncertain until experimentally validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of alloy samples of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 with varying Hf levels (0, 1, 2, and 3 atomic percent). Process all samples using the same casting and thermo-mechanical treatment methods. Subject samples to a battery of tests: room-temperature tensile testing, cyclic thermal conditioning up to 700°C, long-term creep tests at elevated temperatures, and corrosion tests in a controlled corrosive atmosphere (e.g., salt spray chamber). Additionally, use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to verify the formation and distribution of HfO2 oxide dispersions.
measurements: Tensile strength and ductility at room temperature
Creep rate and lifespan at high temperatures
Corrosion rate via electrochemical measurements or mass loss assessments
Microstructural analysis confirming the presence, size, and distribution of oxide dispersions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If alloys with added Hf do not show a statistically significant improvement in creep resistance and corrosion stability relative to the control (0% Hf) without suffering a meaningful loss in strength or ductility, or if detrimental phases or embrittlement are observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. reading.lever: Introduce a minor Hf addition to promote in situ formation of stable oxide dispersions.
reading.why: This composition modification, evidenced in refractory and eutectic systems, can directly enhance long-term creep resistance and corrosion stability under extreme conditions.
